The deployment of multiple interacting generative AI models within a single institutioneach capable of updating its own internal parameters in response to market data-creates a new class of ensemble-level risk that lies outside the scope of classical single-model Model Risk Management (MRM). Traditional MRM compliance treats each model as an independent unit: the model owner validates the model, documents its assumptions, monitors its outputs, and attests to conceptual soundness. This paradigm was designed for static or slowly-evolving statistical models. It breaks down, we argue, in the multi-agent generative setting for two reasons. Reason 1: Cross-agent coupling induces hidden correlated drift. When a metalearning parameter Φ t -a shared embedding layer, a common reinforcement-learning reward signal, or a joint fine-tuning objective-influences all K agents simultaneously, each agent's weight update becomes correlated with all others through the coupling matrix A. A small bias h in Φ t propagates through the coupling so that all agents drift in the same direction, even when no single agent's individual drift exceeds its declared threshold. Reason 2: Individual stability does not imply joint stability. Our Theorem 5.1 (Emergent Ensemble Risk) shows rigorously that there exist parameter regimes in which the per-agent Lyapunov function V k (t) = 1 2 W k t 2 satisfies V k (t) ≤ θ ind for every k = 1, . . . , K, while the joint function V (W t ) = k V k (t) exceeds the threshold θ joint = (1 + δ)K E[V k ∞ ] for any δ > 0, when a coordinated hidden drift is present. This is not a pathological corner case: it follows directly from the variance-aggregation structure of independent 1D Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.

We work in continuous time throughout. The stochastic processes are defined on a complete filtered probability space (Ω, F, (F t ) t≥0 , P) satisfying the usual conditions. Brownian motions B 1 , . . . , B K are mutually independent ddimensional standard Wiener processes. All model weights W k ∈ R d are elements of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. We make no claim about the specific architecture of the models; the analysis applies to any system whose weight dynamics are governed by the SDE described in Section 2. Notation. We write ∥•∥ for the Euclidean norm on R d and ∥•∥ F for the Frobenius norm on R d×d . For a matrix A ∈ R K×K , λ max (A) denotes its spectral radius (largest eigenvalue in absolute value) and λ 2 (A) the second-largest eigenvalue. We write λ min (A) for the eigenvalue of A with the smallest (most negative) real part, and A sym = 1 2 (A + A ⊤ ) for the symmetric part with smallest eigenvalue λ min (A sym ). The exact second-moment stability threshold is governed by λ min (A) (the spectral abscissa of the joint drift operator); the quadratic-Lyapunov sufficient certificate is governed by λ min (A sym ). These coincide when A is normal and differ otherwise; neither is λ max (A), which is identically 1 for every row-stochastic A by Perron-Frobenius. We use ⟨u, v⟩ for the standard inner product on R d .

Section 2 defines the multi-agent SDE and its standing assumptions. Section 3 develops the joint Lyapunov theory, culminating in the Stability Theorem and the Noise-Floor Theorem. Section 4 analyzes the stability threshold and proves the critical coupling formula. Section 6 constructs the ZK-SNARK. Section 7 gives a detailed treatment of the MRM mapping. Section 8 presents five numerical studies. Section 9 discusses implications and Section 10 concludes.

The system (2) assigns each agent a state W k t ∈ R d evolving as a diffusion, and every result in this paper -the critical coupling γ * (A) of (12), the noise floor (17), and the spectral certificate -is a statement about that diffusion. Since the intended application is to ensembles of large generative models, whose parameter counts run to 10 9 -10 12 , we state explicitly what W k t is meant to denote and what the results do not assert. W k t is an effective coordinate. The analysis nowhere requires d to be an agent's full parameter count. It requires only that the governed adaptation of agent k be representable as a diffusion on R d with a declared diffusion coefficient. In practice W k t is intended to be one of: the parameters of a low-rank adapter or head, where continual adaptation is confined; a projection of the parameter vector onto a subspace fixed at validation time; or a declared vector-valued summary statistic of the agent's state. All theorems hold verbatim under any of these readings; what changes is the meaning of d, and therefore of every constant that scales with it. What the literal reading would require. Reading W k t as an agent's raw parameter vector is not something we defend, for three reasons.

First, Assumption 2.1 sets ∇L k (w) = α self w, so the loss is the isotropic quadratic 1 2 α self ∥w∥ 2 , minimized at the origin. For a generative model the origin is not a desirable state but a destroyed one; the mean-reverting term of ( 5) is therefore best read as a regularization force -weight decay, or a pull toward a validated reference point after recentering -and not as descent on a task loss. The task-loss gradient does not appear in the model at all. Second, the isotropy is severe. A single scalar α self stands in for the entire curvature structure, whereas the loss geometry of a large model is strongly anisotropic. Under an effective-coordinate reading this is far less demanding: one may choose the coordinate precisely so that the local curvature is approximately isotropic on it, which is not available in the raw parameter space. Third, the constants scale with d. The noise floor (17) is E π [V ] = Kdσ 2 0 /(4α self ), linear in d. At d ∼ 10 11 the absolute magnitude of this quantity is not meaningful as a risk level; only ratios and thresholds normalized by Kd retain interpretation. Reported in an effective coordinate of modest dimension, it is directly interpretable. What survives regardless of the reading. Two of the paper's conclusions are insensitive to how W k t is interpreted, because they concern the coupling, not the state. The critical threshold γ * (A) = α self / |λ min (A)| depends on d not at all; it is a statement about the interaction matrix and the self-decay rate. Likewise the topology ordering -that stability is governed by the most negative eigenvalue of A rather than by its spectral radius or spectral gap -is a property of A alone. These are the results we regard as the paper's contribution, and they are exactly the ones that do not inherit the scale problem.

Relation to the stated limitations. This reading does not dissolve the linearity and homogeneity assumptions discussed in Section 7.6; it relocates them. Under an effective-coordinate reading the question becomes whether the induced process on the chosen coordinate is approximately linear with approximately homogeneous decay -a local and testable question, rather than a global claim about the loss surface of a large model. We do not test it here, and the numerical studies of Section 8 simulate the model of Section 2 directly rather than any projection of a trained network.

Stability is a property of a well-defined process, so the analysis begins by confirming the coupled K-agent system has a unique solution to be stable about. This guarantee is what licenses speaking of a single joint trajectory at all-and hence of ensemble-level dynamics, rather than K separate agent-by-agent ones. Proposition 2.4 (Well-posedness). Under Assumptions 2.1-2.3, the SDE (2)-(4) admits a unique strong solution {W t } t≥0 for every initial condition W 0 ∈ R dK . The solution is a Markov process with respect to the filtration (F t ) t≥0 . Proof. It suffices to verify the standard Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions for SDEs; see, e.g., [1] Theorem 5.2.1. The drift µ k in (5) is affine in W, hence globally Lipschitz with constant L = α self + γ ∥A∥ F . The diffusion σ(W k ) = σ 0 I d is constant and hence trivially Lipschitz. Linear growth holds since µ k (W) ≤ (α self + γ) ∥W∥ + γΦ max , which is bounded by C(1 + ∥W∥) for large enough C > 0. Existence, uniqueness, and the Markov property follow from [1].

Theorem 3.7 gives a sufficient stability certificate γ < γ cert (A) = α self / |λ min (A sym )|. We now determine the exact threshold and identify the mode that goes unstable. The key structural fact is that the system is a linear (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) diffusion, so both its mean and its second moment are stable if and only if the joint drift operator is positivestable. This is the central result of the paper. The threshold γ * (A) is a critical governance threshold : a hard, topology-dependent ceiling on how tightly a population of models may be coupled before interconnection alone tips the ensemble from a stable regime into one whose risk grows without bound. It is, in principle, a governance limit of the same character as a position or concentration limit-an observable threshold on a structural quantity-and, as the remark above stresses, it is governed by the system's disagreement mode, not the consensus mode that per-model intuition would lead one to monitor. , the mode along the λ min (A) eigenvector is marginally stable and E[V (W t )] grows linearly in t, so no stationary distribution exists. Remark 4.3 (On terminology: a stability threshold, not a phase transition). Earlier drafts described the behavior at γ * (A) as a phase transition. We avoid that term. What Theorem 4.2 establishes is the crossing of an eigenvalue of the joint drift operator through zero: for γ < γ * the operator M is positive-stable and a stationary law exists; at γ = γ * the leading eigenvalue reaches the imaginary axis; above it, the second moment grows without bound. This is linear (in)stability of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck system, and it is exactly and analytically solvable. It has none of the features that give the physical term its content -there is no order parameter, no critical exponent, no non-analyticity of a free energy, and no thermodynamic limit. The transition is sharp in γ simply because the real part of an eigenvalue is a continuous function that changes sign at a point. We retain the language of a critical coupling because γ * is a genuine threshold with governance meaning, but the mathematics behind it is an eigenvalue computation, and we do not want the terminology to suggest otherwise.

The ordering has a concrete governance reading: the topology of interconnection is itself a control variable. A complete, densely diversified coupling tolerates the most shared adaptation before destabilizing, while a star-a single dominant hub on which all others depend-tolerates the least, so the same total coupling strength can be safe in one architecture and supercritical in another. Ensemble structure, not merely coupling magnitude, is therefore a lever the governance function can act on.

One of the most important motivations for the JLP over per-agent MRM is that individual stability does not imply joint stability under coordinated hidden drift. We formalize this claim. This is the rigorous form of the premise motivating ensemble-level governance-that a collection of individually sound models can nonetheless compose a fragile systemtransposed to a population of self-adapting models.

Theorem 5.1 establishes an exact window δ ∈ (0, 1) in which hidden coordinated drift is invisible to individual MRM but detectable by the JLP. The width of the window in δ does not depend on K; what improves with K is the precision of the joint estimate, since V joint averages the same coordinated signal over more agents. Throughout the window ∥h∥ is small relative to σ 0 : each agent's drift stays below its individual noise floor while the collective signal exceeds the joint threshold. Numerical Study C5 exhibits this phenomenon concretely with K = 10, h per dim = 0.00935, σ 0 = 0.05, confirming that 0/10 agents are individually flagged while the joint check fires. In governance terms this is the paper's central cautionary result: a validation regime that certifies each model in isolation can pass an entire population while the ensemble they constitute drifts together past its joint tolerance. The joint monitor that closes the gap is an aggregate of the very same per-model Lyapunov quantities a per-model regime already computes-what changes is not the data collected but that it is assessed jointly, at the level of the ensemble.

p.s: The Spectral Certificate and Its Circuit
p.t: If the topology A is not itself confidential, the certificate γ < α self / |λ min (A)| is checked directly from the declared model documentation and needs no proof system. The ZK machinery becomes relevant only when A (or γ) is proprietary. In that case the firm commits to A and proves, in zero knowledge, a spectral statement about the committed matrix: where A sym = 1 2 (A + A ⊤ ). The positive-definiteness α self I + γA sym ≻ 0 is equivalent to γ < γ cert (A), the safe (conservative) certificate; it is the natural object to prove because it is decidable by a Cholesky factorization, which a circuit can verify without computing eigenvalues. (Attesting the exact γ < γ * (A) instead requires bounding λ min (A) of the committed, possibly non-symmetric A; we use the conservative certificate precisely because it is SNARK-friendly and never certifies an unstable system.) Crucially, (22) has no W t argument: it is proved once when the firm declares or changes its coupling configuration, not at every monitoring epoch. The weight-commitment clause Hash(•) = H is retained, but its role is now correctly scoped: it provides tamper-evidence and non-repudiation for the declared configuration (A, γ), and is orthogonal to stability. A separate, genuinely state-dependent monitoring signal-if one is wanted at each epoch-is whether the realized Lyapunov value V (W τn ) stays within the stationary envelope β/α eff of (16); that is a meaningful per-epoch check because it can fail, unlike the pointwise generator inequality.

The statement (22) is converted to an arithmetic circuit over a prime field F p as follows. The witness is the committed matrix A (equivalently its symmetric part S := α self I K + γA sym ) together with a claimed Cholesky factor L; there are no model weights in the circuit. Step 2: Verify the Cholesky factorization S = LL ⊤ . The prover supplies a lowertriangular L as private witness; the circuit checks LL ⊤ = S entrywise (O(K 3 ) multiplications) and that each diagonal entry L ii is nonzero. A real Cholesky factor with nonzero (hence, by the field encoding, positive) diagonal exists iff S ≻ 0, i.e. iff γ < γ cert (A). This replaces an eigenvalue computation, which is not circuit-friendly, by a verification of an algebraic identity.

A Poseidon hash H(A, γ, Key) over F p binds the committed configuration to the ledger entry. Poseidon is SNARK-friendly with low gate count [6]. This clause provides tamper-evidence for (A, γ) and is independent of the stability claim.

The three properties below are what make the certificate usable as governance reporting. Soundness means a model owner cannot fake compliance with the ensemble-stability threshold; completeness means a genuinely compliant owner can always demonstrate it; and zero-knowledge means it can do so without disclosing its proprietary coupling matrix. Together they resolve the central tension in collecting ensemble-level information: the validation function learns whether each model sits on the stable side of γ * , and can aggregate these attestations, without any party pooling the sensitive models whose very concentration would create a new exposure. Proposition 6.2 (Soundness and completeness of π JLP ). Let R be the NP relation defined by statement (22): a pair (A, γ) with a valid witness L such that LL ⊤ = α self I K + γA sym has strictly positive diagonal, together with the hash binding. A ZK-SNARK with the following properties can be instantiated using the Groth16 construction [5]: (i) Completeness. If γ < γ cert (A) the certifying Cholesky factor exists and the prover can always generate a valid proof π JLP . (ii) Soundness. With overwhelming probability, no polynomial-time prover can produce a valid π JLP when α self I + γA sym ̸ ≻ 0 (no real Cholesky factor with positive diagonal exists), i.e. the certificate cannot be forged for an uncertified configuration.

(iii) Zero-knowledge. The proof reveals no information about the committed A beyond the membership statement. Proof. All three properties follow from the Groth16 construction for rank-1 constraint systems (R1CS), the standard encoding for the arithmetic circuit above. The circuit size is O(K 3 ) constraints (dominated by the Cholesky-identity check), polynomial in K and independent of the model dimension d and of the live weights, and hence admits an efficient prover. Soundness of the algebraic check reduces to the fact that S ≻ 0 iff a Cholesky factor with positive diagonal exists; we refer to [5] for the formal SNARK security proof under the generic group model. Governance ledger integration. When the firm declares or changes its coupling configuration, it: (a) commits to (A, γ) on the ledger; (b) generates π JLP proving the spectral certificate and the hash binding; (c) submits (π JLP , H) to the governance ledger. The validator runs the polynomial-time verifier V, which accepts or rejects without ever seeing A. Per-epoch telemetry, if required, reports only whether V (W τn ) remains within the (i) That V is a meaningful proxy for ensemble-level model risk: large V indicates that aggregate model weights have drifted far from their validated origin, which corresponds to distributional shift in the models' outputs. (ii) That the coupling matrix A accurately reflects the institution's actual model interaction topology (shared fine-tuning datasets, shared embedding layers, common RLHF reward signals).

(iii) That the declared parameters α self , σ 0 , γ, and Φ are calibrated to observed weight dynamics during a supervised validation period, not set arbitrarily. (iv) That the critical threshold γ * (A) derived in Theorem 4.2 has been computed for the declared topology and that the institution's operational γ satisfies γ < γ * (A) with a documented safety margin. This maps directly to the MRM requirement that model developers should be able to explain why a particular mathematical approach was selected and what its limitations are. Pillar 2: Ongoing Monitoring. MRM requires that models be monitored continuously against performance benchmarks and that deviations trigger escalation procedures. The JLP provides a natural and continuous monitoring framework. At each epoch τ n (e.g., daily), the firm submits a ZK proof π JLP that LV (W τn ) < -α eff V (W τn ) + β. This is equivalent to certifying that the joint system is within its stability envelope as characterized by Theorem 3.7. The key features of this monitoring framework are: (i) Continuous attestation: unlike annual validation exercises, the JLP provides daily cryptographic attestations stored on the governance ledger, creating an auditready tamper-evident record. (ii) Early warning: the sequence {V (W τn )} ∞ n=0 forms a real-valued time series whose trend can be monitored with standard process-control methods (CUSUM, EWMA). An upward trend in V signals incipient instability before the stability bound is formally violated.

(iii) Granular decomposition: the exact generator formula (9) decomposes the total risk into self-decay (first term), coupling (second term), and noise (third term), allowing examiners to identify which component is driving elevated V . (iv) Noise floor calibration: Theorem 3.8 provides a closed-form baseline E[V ∞ ] = β 0 /(2α self ) against which current V can be compared, making the monitoring threshold explicit and auditable. Pillar 3: Model Validation. MRM requires independent model validation (MV) by a function separate from model development. The guidance specifies three components of validation: evaluation of conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and outcomes analysis. The JLP enhances validation in the multi-agent context in three ways. First, the MV function can independently verify the topology declaration by examining shared infrastructure: fine-tuning pipelines, embedding layers, and reward-signal configurations. Second, the historical sequence of π JLP proofs on the ledger provides an objective record for outcomes analysis-the MV function checks not only that proofs were submitted but that the underlying V trajectory was consistent with the declared dynamics parameters. Third, the governance injection probe described in Section 8 (Numerical Study C4) provides a challenge procedure: the examiner injects a known perturbation ∆ to the metaparameter Φ t and verifies that the JLP telemetry responds as predicted by the certified dynamics within the detection horizon.

During the initial validation period (e.g. 90-180 days), the self-decay rate α self , noise coefficient σ 0 , and coupling strength γ are estimated from observed weight trajectories using the moment-matching conditions of Theorems 3.8 and 3.7. The critical threshold γ * (A) is computed and documented. Stage 3: Validation of the JLP Circuit. The model validation function independently audits the arithmetic circuit described in Section 6, verifying that the circuit correctly encodes the stability condition from Theorem 3.7. This audit is analogous to the standard "back-testing" requirement but adapted to the ZK-SNARK context.

Linear dynamics, and homogeneity across agents. This is the strongest modeling restriction in the paper and it underlies every exact result, so we state it first. Assumption 2.1 takes each agent's loss to be exactly the isotropic quadratic L k (w) = 1 2 α self ∥w∥ 2 , with the same α self for every agent, and the coupling in (3) is linear in W with additive, state-independent noise. The joint process is therefore a linear multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. That is precisely why the analysis closes in the form it does: the exact threshold γ * (A) = α self / |λ min (A)| is the point at which an eigenvalue of a constant drift matrix crosses zero; the noise floor E π [V ] = Kdσ 2 0 /(4α self ) is the stationary second moment of a Gaussian; and the spectral certificate is a statement about a fixed symmetric matrix. None of these survives unchanged for a non-convex, anisotropic, or agent-heterogeneous loss landscape -which is what the loss surfaces of actual generative models are. Three consequences deserve emphasis. First, α self is not a property one reads off a deployed model; it is the curvature of an assumed quadratic, and for a real system it would have to be estimated locally, with the results holding only in whatever neighborhood that local approximation is credible. Second, heterogeneous α (k) self would replace the scalar threshold by a condition on a non-uniformly scaled operator, and the clean eigenvalue characterization would become an inequality rather than an identity. Third, non-convexity admits multiple basins, so "the" stationary distribution is replaced by basin-dependent behavior and the global statements above become local ones.

We therefore read this paper's contribution as a tractable idealization that isolates one mechanism -how coupling topology governs the stability of an interacting ensemble -and makes it exactly computable, not as a description of the dynamics of production generative models. Extending the threshold to locally-quadratic or heterogeneous settings is the most consequential open problem we leave.

The quadratic V (W) = 1 2 k W k 2 is analytically tractable but may not capture all relevant risk dimensions for generative models (e.g., distributional shift in output space, not parameter space). Future work should consider Lyapunov functions based on output divergence metrics (KL, MMD, Wasserstein). Non-stationary meta-parameters. We assumed Φ t is fixed. In practice, Φ t may itself be updated by a higher-level learning process, introducing non-stationarity that invalidates the stationary distribution results. Adversarial meta-parameters. The ZK-SNARK proves that W t satisfies the stability condition at epoch τ n , but it does not prevent the firm from manipulating Φ t between epochs. Continuous Φ t monitoring (via the injection probe of Study C4) partially mitigates this, but a fully adversarial Φ t scenario requires stronger proof systems.

We validate the theoretical claims of Sections 3-5 through five numerical studies (C1-C5) implemented in Python (NumPy). All simulations use Euler-Maruyama discretization with step size ∆t = 0.01. Seeds are fixed and documented, so every figure and table is exactly reproducible; in Study C3, where several parameter configurations are compared, the seeds additionally depend on the configuration so that the comparisons are statistically independent rather than deterministic rescalings of one another. Scope of the numerical evidence. These are verification experiments for an analytically solvable model, and their limits should be read into every number below. (i) Monte Carlo dispersion is reported only for Study C3, where n mc = 30 paths per configuration permit a standard error; the remaining studies report single-path or single-configuration point estimates without error bars, so their trailing digits are not significant. (ii) Ensemble sizes are small -K = 5 throughout except K = 10 in Study C5 -and the topology comparison of Study C2 is conducted at K = 5 only, so the ordering complete > ring > star is demonstrated at one ensemble size rather than established as a general scaling law. (iii) No step-size convergence study is performed; discretization bias at ∆t = 0.01 is not quantified. (iv) Most importantly, the simulated system is the model of Section 2a linear Ornstein-Uhlenbeck ensemble -so these studies verify that our analysis of that model is correct. They are not evidence that production model ensembles obey it; that would require the linearity and homogeneity assumptions discussed in Section 7.6 to hold empirically, which we do not test. Interpretation. Three findings emerge. First, α eff (γ) is a strictly decreasing function of γ (from 0.264 at γ = 0 to -0.049 at γ = 0.50), confirming that coupling reduces-and eventually reverses-the effective decay rate. Second, the residual LV + 2α self V grows rapidly with γ (from 0.018 to 4.671), confirming Corollary 3.6: the naive bound fails as soon as γ > 0. Third, β eff remains at exactly β naive = 0.02500 for all stable γ, confirming that the noise floor formula is exact and the coupling affects only α eff . Note that the complete-graph run is still stable at γ = 0.30 ( V ≈ 0.50) and only blows up between γ = 0.40 and 0.50, consistent with the exact threshold γ * = α self / |λ min (A)| = 0.10/0.25 = 0.40 for the complete graph (Table 2)-not the 0.20 that the original 2α self /λ max formula would give. The implication for MRM is direct: a firm that declares the naive decay rate α eff = 2α self = 0.20 while operating at γ = 0.20 is overstating its effective decay rate by a factor of two (0.2642 → 0.1015), which translates to an underestimate of the time required to return to the stability envelope after a shock.

p.s: Study C2: Critical Coupling by Topology
p.t: Design. For each topology we measure the empirical critical coupling two ways. (a) A divergence sweep: we sweep γ, run T = 3,000 steps with the meta-parameter present, and record the steady-state V (declaring divergence when the last-200-step mean exceeds 500); this produces the V (γ) curves in Figure 1. (b) A growth-rate crossing: for the homogeneous system (Φ = 0) we project onto the λ min (A) eigenmode and estimate the late-time exponential growth rate of its second moment, locating γ * emp where it crosses zero. Method (b) isolates the marginal mode from the noise floor and recovers the asymptotic threshold cleanly; the lenient fixed-horizon divergence test of method (a) overshoots it (a finite run has not yet blown up just above γ * ). What this study does and does not show is worth stating plainly. The system is a linear Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process whose stability threshold is available in closed form, so C2 is a check that the simulation and the algebra agree -it confirms the arithmetic and the implementation, and it rules out sign or scaling errors in γ * (A). It is not independent evidence that real model ensembles exhibit this threshold, since the threshold's existence follows from the linearity assumed in Assumption 2.1 rather than being discovered empirically. Its value is that the ordering by |λ min (A)|, and the failure of the spectral radius to predict it, are both non-obvious and are borne out numerically.

p.s: Study C2: Critical Coupling by Topology
p.t: The MRM implication is that two institutions with identical K, α self , and γ may face very different ensemble-level risk depending solely on their interaction topology, and that the quantity to declare and bound is |λ min (A)|-not the spectral radius, and not the second eigenvalue λ 2 that the original analysis tabulated.

Design. We set γ = 0 and Φ = 0 and measure V = E[V ∞ ] across n mc = 30 independent paths per configuration. Eight configurations span (K, d, σ 0 ) ∈ {3, 5, 8} × {2, 4, 8} × {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20} (selected subset). The seeds are drawn from a deterministic hash of the configuration as well as the path index, so the runs remain exactly reproducible while the eight configurations are statistically independent of one another. This matters more than it might appear. With a configuration-independent seed sequence, the linearity of (2) at γ = 0 with additive noise and a σ 0 -scaled initial condition gives the pathwise identity W t (σ 0 ) = (σ 0 /σ ′ 0 ) W t (σ ′ 0 ), so V would scale as σ 2 0 by construction and the three σ 0 -varying rows would be deterministic rescalings of a single run rather than independent tests -reporting an error of exactly 0.0% that reflects arithmetic, not agreement. Decoupling the seeds removes that artifact, at the cost of larger and more honest residuals. Table 3: C3: Empirical noise floor V ∞ vs. theory β 0 /(2α self ), over n mc = 30 independent paths per configuration. σ mc is the sample standard deviation across paths, SE = σ mc / √ n mc the standard error of the mean, and

Interpretation. Empirical values match theory to within Monte Carlo error across all eight configurations: relative errors run from 0.17% to 5.33%, and in standard-error units the largest discrepancy is z = 1.55, with 5/8 configurations inside one standard error and 8/8 inside two. Two points about how this comparison is made. First, the agreement test uses the standard error of the mean SE = σ mc / √ n mc , not the path-to-path standard deviation σ mc . Testing a sample mean against σ mc would be too lenient by a factor √ n mc and would declare agreement almost regardless of the data; the z column reports the honest quantity. Second, because the σ 0 rows are now seeded independently (see Design), they constitute a genuine test of the σ 2 0 scaling rather than an identity: their errors (0.23%, 2.01%, 2.59%) are ordinary sampling residuals, and it is the fact that they are small across a hundredfold range of β 0 (0.004 to 0.40) that carries the evidential weight. Subject to that, the formula scales linearly in K, d, and σ 2 0 as predicted, enabling the model owner to predict the stationary risk level from declared system parameters-a prerequisite for setting monitoring thresholds. The scaling is verified over K ∈ {3, 5, 8}, d ∈ {2, 4, 8} and σ 0 ∈ [0.02, 0.20]; extrapolation far outside those ranges is not tested here.

p.s: Study C4: Governance Φ t Injection Probe
p.t: Design. We simulate the complete-graph system with K = 5 for a burn-in of T pre = 2,000 steps, then inject a step perturbation ∆Φ at t = 20 (after burn-in). The perturbed meta-parameter has magnitude ∥Φ + ∆Φ∥ = 2 ∥Φ∥ nominal . For each γ ∈ {0.05, 0.20, 0.50}, we measure the change in LV (pre-vs. post-probe, 100-step rolling window) and the steps to 3σ detection. Interpretation. Two regimes emerge. At γ = 0.20, the probe is detected in just 13 steps (0.13 time units)-a fast and unambiguous response. At γ = 0.50, the larger ∆LV is offset by higher baseline variance, giving detection at 183 steps. At γ = 0.05, the coupling is too weak to propagate the perturbation through the network within the measurement window; detection requires > 2,000 steps (20 time units). This study has a direct MRM implication for the Effective Challenge pillar. The validator must declare the minimum γ min required for the injection probe to be a valid challenge procedure. Based on the numerical results, we recommend γ min = 0.20 as a practical lower bound for the probe to be informative within a 1-day horizon. Institutions operating at γ < γ min should be required to use alternative challenge procedures (e.g., direct weight inspection under confidentiality agreement). Why γ = 0.50 is slower than γ = 0.20. This is not a contradiction. At high γ, the system is closer to the phase boundary and exhibits higher variance in LV ; the signal-tonoise ratio is lower even though the absolute ∆LV is larger. The detection time scales as τ detect ∝ Var(LV )/(∆LV ) 2 , and the variance grows faster than the signal near the phase boundary. This suggests that the optimal probe design should account for the signal-to-noise tradeoff and may prefer moderate γ to extremes.

Design. This is the central study of the paper. We set K = 10, d = 4, γ = 0 (worst case: no coupling, so the JLP is acting on purely additive drift), and T = 400,000 steps (T = 4,000 time units). This long run is necessary because the OU correlation time is τ corr = 1/(2α self ) = 5 time units, giving T /(2τ corr ) = 400 effective samples per agent for robust time-averaging. The hidden drift is h i = h per dim in every dimension of every agent, with magnitude chosen to place each agent's steady-state E[V k ] in the "individual-pass" zone: This design satisfies (21) with δ = 0.70: 4α self = 0.0175 + 0.0250 = 0.0425, while the individual threshold is θ ind = 2 × 0.0249 = 0.0498 (where 0.0249 is the measured honest mean, in close agreement with the theoretical 0.0250). Per-agent detail. The steady-state mean V k for each of the 10 attack agents (over T = 4,000 time units) is: 0.040, 0.044, 0.044, 0.043, 0.036, 0.041, 0.040, 0.042, 0.041, 0.044. All are below the individual threshold 0.04977. The joint sum is 0.414 > 0.373. This has a striking practical implication: decommissioning a centralized "AI hub" (star, γ * = 0.10) in favor of a fully-connected mesh (complete, γ * = 0.40) quadruples the network's stable coupling range. Conversely, institutions that centralize model orchestration through a single meta-learning server are implicitly operating with a star topology and should apply correspondingly tighter coupling constraints. The number to compute, declare, and bound is |λ min (A)|.

p.s: The Noise-Floor Formula as an Audit Anchor
p.t: Theorem 3.8 provides a closed-form baseline V th ∞ = Kdσ 2 0 /(4α self ) that can be computed from declared system parameters alone. Numerical Study C3 confirms this formula to within < 8% across a wide range of (K, d, σ 0 ). This formula serves as an audit anchor : before any model is deployed, the institution declares (α self , σ 0 , K, d) and the validator computes V th ∞ . If the firm's submitted V values are systematically below V th ∞ , this indicates that the declared σ 0 or α self is overstated-a potential form of concealed model adaptation.

Having corrected the attestation target to the static spectral certificate (Section 6), the question is whether zero knowledge is still needed-couldn't the firm just disclose (A, γ) under a confidentiality agreement? The coupling topology A encodes which models share fine-tuning data, embeddings, and reward signals, and is itself competitively sensitive; the same three arguments apply, now about A rather than the weights. First, confidentiality agreements do not prevent leakage through side-channels: staff who see the declared topology may inadvertently or deliberately reveal architectural information to competitors or the press. Second, the SNARK provides non-repudiation: the firm cannot later claim that a certified configuration differed from the deployed one, since the proof is bound to the committed (A, γ) by the hash clause. This is valuable in enforcement actions. Third, the approach scales to multiple reviewers: the model owner submits the same certificate to several independent oversight functions simultaneously without any of them seeing A. Because the certificate is proved once per configuration rather than at every epoch, the cryptographic cost is incurred rarely.

The JLP generator value LV (W t ) is a natural input to CUSUM (Cumulative Sum) process-control charts, which are widely used in MRM for detecting persistent shifts in model performance. Define where κ > 0 is the allowance parameter. The CUSUM alarm fires when S n > h CUSUM for some threshold h CUSUM . This detects persistent upward shifts in LV earlier than singlepoint threshold tests, and its ARL (average run length) properties are well-understood.

We have developed and validated a complete mathematical framework for the governance of K-agent self-adapting generative AI systems under MRM. The framework proceeds in four steps. Step 1 (Generator): Theorem 3.3 gives the exact formula for the infinitesimal generator LV of the joint quadratic Lyapunov function. This formula shows that the naive self-decay bound α eff = 2α self fails immediately upon introduction of coupling (γ > 0), and that the excess is driven by the cross-agent inner products ⟨W k , Φ -W j ⟩. Step 3 (Emergent Risk): Theorem 5.1 and Numerical Study C5 demonstrate that with K = 10 agents and a small coordinated hidden drift (h per dim = 0.00935), all 10 individual Lyapunov monitors remain below their thresholds while the joint Lyapunov monitor fires. This is the fundamental justification for the JLP over per-agent MRM.

We show that a per-epoch SNARK proving the pointwise generator inequality at the live weights is vacuous (Proposition 6.1), and retarget the attestation at the static spectral certificate α self I + γA sym ≻ 0 on a committed (possibly proprietary) coupling matrix, proved once per configuration via a Cholesky factorization with O(K 3 ) circuit complexity and no dependence on live weights. The mapping to MRM (Section 7) covers all three pillars of the guidance: Conceptual Soundness (justification of V , A, and parameter calibration), Ongoing Monitoring (per-configuration spectral certificates plus envelope checks V (W τn ) ≤ β/α eff on the governance ledger), and Model Validation (independent audit of the ZK circuit and injection probe procedures). Future work will address the non-quadratic (weighted) Lyapunov certificates that would close the normal/non-normal gap up to γ * (A), non-stationary meta-parameters, and adversarial Φ t manipulation scenarios.
